Closing one end of an organ pipe alters the harmonics produced by transforming it from an
open pipe to a closed pipe. In an open pipe, both ends allow for the formation of standing
waves with both odd and even harmonics, while a closed pipe, which has one end closed and
one end open, only supports odd harmonics. This is because the closed end must be a node
(point of no displacement) and the open end must be an antinode (point of maximum
displacement). As a result, harmonics that are even multiples, such as the second and
fourth harmonics, will be absent in a closed pipe configuration. Thus, the transition from
an open to a closed pipe significantly impacts the harmonic spectrum, restricting it to
only the fundamental frequency and its odd harmonics.
answers.explanation: correct because closing one end of an organ pipe changes its harmonic structure from supporting both odd and even harmonics in an open pipe to only allowing odd harmonics in a closed pipe, due to the requirement of having a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end.

speed of sound is reduced by 3%, we first need to determine the standard speed of sound at
room temperature, which is approximately 343 m/s. A 3% reduction results in a new speed of

harmonic) is given by the formula f = v / (2 L), where v is the speed of sound and L is
the length of the pipe. Assuming a standard pipe length of 1 meter, the resonant frequency
would then be approximately 166.75 Hz. However, for a more specific case or a provided
pipe length that leads to the key answer of 427 Hz, we can deduce that the length would
have to be about 0.39 meters. Thus, with the adjusted speed of sound, the resonant
frequency of the pipe on a cold day is calculated to be 427 Hz.
